strings.path.title: Arpeggios over Changes
strings.path.goal: Play the notes of each chord of a progression as a line, in time, moving to the nearest note of the next chord, and take the first steps into sweeping them.
strings.path.assumes: You can play major and minor triads in three shapes and the four-string shapes from the last Level of Triads, and you know the chords of a key by number: the first Level of Chords in a Key. The twelve-bar form and two, five, one are spelled out where they are used. Eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM. No sweep picking is assumed. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; arpeggios are something players practise for years.
strings.path.gradingLimits: After the take the app checks the single-note lines for right notes, counts them and times them. The note check only works when notes are separate: lift each finger as the next lands, or it reads 'not checked'. The app cannot tell which string a pitch came from. The sweeps in the last Level are timed and counted and never pitch-checked, because swept strings ring together and a correct take could read as wrong; whether each note was clean is for your ear, and the Exercise asks you. The band Exercises have only been tried on computer-made guitar sound, so direct input or headphones are the honest way to play them. Choosing your own notes is 'your turn', self-checked and labelled 'not checked yet'.
strings.path.skills.0: Triads in three shapes on the top strings
strings.path.skills.1: Eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM
strings.step.one-octave.title: A chord as a line
strings.step.one-octave.goal: Play C major and A minor as arpeggios: root, third, fifth and the root above, one note on each of four strings, up and back.
strings.step.one-octave.why: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time, in order. You have been doing something close to it since Triads, rolling shapes. The difference, in this Path, is in the fretting hand: in a rolled chord the fingers stay down and the notes ring together, and here each finger lets go as the next note sounds, so it comes out as a line you could sing. Lines are what solos and melodies are made of, and a line made of a chord's own notes always fits that chord.
strings.step.one-octave.howTo.0: The shape starts from the root on the D string and takes one note on each string up to the top: root, third, fifth, root.
strings.step.one-octave.howTo.1: C major: D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 8. A minor: D string 7, then fret 5 on the G, B and top strings.
strings.step.one-octave.howTo.2: Where two notes share a fret, lay the first finger flat and roll it from one string to the next so the first note stops as the second starts.
strings.step.one-octave.payoff: C and A minor as lines, one octave each, with every note separate.
strings.exercise.one-octave.c-major.title: C major, one octave
strings.exercise.one-octave.c-major.purpose: Root, third, fifth, root: C, E, G and the C above, one note a string, then back down to the low C.
strings.exercise.one-octave.c-major.howTo.0: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
strings.exercise.one-octave.c-major.howTo.1: Up: D string 10 (third finger), G string 9 (second), B string 8 and top string 8 (first finger, rolled). Down: B string 8, G string 9, and the D string held for two beats.
strings.exercise.one-octave.c-major.howTo.2: Let each note go as you play the next. If two notes ring together it is a chord again.
strings.exercise.one-octave.c-major.coachLine: Right notes and steady quarters after the take. Notes that ring into each other can read as not checked.
strings.exercise.one-octave.a-minor.title: A minor, one octave
strings.exercise.one-octave.a-minor.purpose: The same idea with a minor chord: A, C, E and the A above. The third is one fret lower than it would be in a major shape, and that puts three notes on one fret.
strings.exercise.one-octave.a-minor.howTo.0: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
strings.exercise.one-octave.a-minor.howTo.1: Up: D string 7 (third finger), then fret 5 on the G, B and top strings, all with the first finger rolled across. Down: B string 5, G string 5, and the D string held for two beats.
strings.exercise.one-octave.a-minor.coachLine: Right notes and steady quarters after the take. The roll across fret 5 is the thing to get clean.
strings.exercise.one-octave.major-and-minor.titl: C and A minor, in eighths
strings.exercise.one-octave.major-and-minor.purp: Both arpeggios over a band, a bar each, up to the top and back. The hand moves three frets between them.
strings.exercise.one-octave.major-and-minor.howT: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar on each chord: C, A minor, C, A minor.
Each bar goes up the four strings, back down to the root on the D string, and adds one more note on the G string. C starts at fret 10 on the D string, A minor at fret 7.
strings.exercise.one-octave.major-and-minor.coac: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.one-octave.major-and-minor.dete: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.step.four-chords.title: An arpeggio for every chord
strings.step.four-chords.goal: Find the root of C, A minor, F and G on the D string and play each chord's arpeggio from it, over a band.
strings.step.four-chords.why: To play arpeggios over a song you need to know, at every bar line, where the next chord's root is. On one string that is easy to see: C at fret 10, A at fret 7, F at fret 3, G at fret 5. Starting every bar on the root is not how the best lines go, but it is how you make sure you always know which chord you are on, and it is where everyone starts.
strings.step.four-chords.howTo.0: Roots on the D string: C is fret 10, A is fret 7, F is fret 3, G is fret 5.
strings.step.four-chords.howTo.1: Major chords (C, F, G) use the shape that goes down a fret on each of the next two strings and then stays: 10, 9, 8, 8. The minor chord (A minor) uses 7, 5, 5, 5.
strings.step.four-chords.howTo.2: Let the last note of each bar be short and move the hand in that gap, so the next bar starts on the click.
strings.step.four-chords.payoff: One, six, four, five as four arpeggios, each starting on its root.
strings.exercise.four-chords.roots.title: The four roots on the D string
strings.exercise.four-chords.roots.purpose: Only the roots, two to a bar, so you know where the hand has to be before the notes above arrive.
strings.exercise.four-chords.roots.howTo.0: Half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. D string, third finger: fret 10, fret 7, fret 3, fret 5.
strings.exercise.four-chords.roots.howTo.1: Say the chord's name as you land on it: C, A minor, F, G.
strings.exercise.four-chords.roots.coachLine: Band on. Eight notes, each the right root, each on time.
strings.exercise.four-chords.roots.detection.0: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.four-chords.up-and-down.title: Up one chord, down the next
strings.exercise.four-chords.up-and-down.purpose: Quarter notes: C going up, A minor coming down, F going up, G coming down. Each bar starts on the string where the last one ended; only the hand moves along it.
strings.exercise.four-chords.up-and-down.howTo.0: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
strings.exercise.four-chords.up-and-down.howTo.1: C up: D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 8. A minor down: fret 5 on the top, B and G strings, then D string 7. F up: 3, 2, 1, 1. G down: top string 3, B string 3, G string 4, D string 5.
strings.exercise.four-chords.up-and-down.coachLi: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.four-chords.up-and-down.detecti: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.four-chords.four-arpeggios.purp: Each chord up to the top string and back, one bar each, with the band. The same line four times in four places.
strings.exercise.four-chords.four-arpeggios.howT: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar on each chord.
C from fret 10 on the D string, A minor from fret 7, F from fret 3, G from fret 5. Each bar ends with one extra note on the G string: use it to look at where the next root is.
strings.exercise.four-chords.four-arpeggios.coac: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.four-chords.four-arpeggios.dete: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.step.nearest-note.title: Start from the nearest note
strings.step.nearest-note.goal: Play through C, A minor, F and G without going back to the root each time: begin each chord on whichever of its notes is closest to where you are.
strings.step.nearest-note.why: Jumping to the root at every bar line makes four separate exercises. Real lines do not jump: when the chord changes, they move to the closest note of the new chord, often the very note they were on. C is a note of C major, of A minor and of F, so a line can sit on it through three chords. This is the same idea as choosing the nearest triad shape, applied to one note at a time, and it is the main thing this Path is for.
strings.step.nearest-note.howTo.0: Before each change, ask which notes the two chords share. C and A minor share C and E. A minor and F share A and C. F and G share none, so there you move by one fret.
strings.step.nearest-note.howTo.1: The line here stays between frets 4 and 10 on the top four strings, and inside the four bars it never jumps more than a string.
strings.step.nearest-note.howTo.2: The last note, B on the G string, is a half step below the C the line starts on, so the ear is led back to the start. The hand has to move from fret 4 up to fret 10 to get there: the only shift in the line.
strings.step.nearest-note.payoff: Four chords played as one line, with no jump from one chord to the next.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.shared-note.title: C into A minor on a shared note
strings.exercise.nearest-note.shared-note.purpos: C major up to its top C, then A minor coming down from that same C. The note does not change when the chord does.
Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. Two bars that loop.
Bar 1, C: D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 8. Bar 2, A minor: top string 8, top string 5, B string 5, G string 5: C, A, E, C.
The C at the top is played twice, once as the root of C and once as the third of A minor.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.shared-note.coachL: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.shared-note.detect: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.title: Four chords, one line
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.purpose: C up, A minor down, F up, G down, each starting on the nearest note of its chord. Four bars with no jump inside them.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.howTo.0: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.howTo.1: Bar 1, C: D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 8. Bar 2, A minor: top string 8 and 5, B string 5, G string 5.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.howTo.2: Bar 3, F: G string 5, B string 6, top string 5 and 8: C, F, A, C. Bar 4, G: top string 7, B string 8, G string 7 and 4: B, G, D, B.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.joined.detection.0: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.title: Your turn: no jumps
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.purpose: C, A minor, F and G with chord notes of your own choosing, one rule: at each change, move to a note of the new chord that is no more than two frets or one string away.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.howTo.0: Quarter notes or any rhythm you like, 60 to 90 BPM, four bars that loop.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.howTo.1: Use only the three notes of each chord. C: C, E, G. A minor: A, C, E. F: F, A, C. G: G, B, D. The written line is one answer.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.howTo.2: Your turn, and not checked yet: the app can't judge notes you choose, so you tick it off yourself.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.coachLin: Not checked yet. Record it and listen for any place where the line leaps.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.detectio: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.nearest-note.your-line.selfChec: Was every note one of the three notes of the chord the band was on?
Did you get through every change without a jump?
strings.step.sevenths.title: Add the seventh
strings.step.sevenths.goal: Play C major seven, A minor seven, D minor seven and G seven as four-note arpeggios, and a line through D minor seven, G seven and C major seven: two, five, one, the second, fifth and first chords of the key.
strings.step.sevenths.why: A seventh chord is a triad with one more note, the seventh note counted from its root. In the shape you know, the top note was the root again. Lower it and you get the seventh instead: one fret down for a major seven, two frets down for a minor seven or a plain seven. Four notes give a line more to say, and they are the sound of jazz, soul and a great deal of pop.
strings.step.sevenths.howTo.0: C major seven is C, E, G, B: D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 7.
strings.step.sevenths.howTo.1: A minor seven is A, C, E, G: D string 7, G string 5, B string 5, top string 3. D minor seven is the same shape from fret 12.
strings.step.sevenths.howTo.2: G seven is G, B, D, F: D string 5, G string 4, B string 3, top string 1. It is the fifth chord of the key: its F wants to fall to E and its B to rise to C, which is what pulls it home.
strings.step.sevenths.howTo.3: The minor seven and plain seven shapes reach five frets. Fourth finger on the D string, first finger on the top string, and let the hand lean toward the first finger: do not hold all four notes down.
strings.step.sevenths.payoff: Four seventh chords as lines, and a two, five, one, the progression jazz players practise most.
strings.exercise.sevenths.major-seven-minor-seve: C major seven and A minor seven
The two arpeggios you know with their top note lowered: B on top of C major, G on top of A minor.
Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar each: C major seven, A minor seven, and again.

C major seven: D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 7, one finger per fret from the fourth down to the first. A minor seven: D string 7 with the fourth finger, G string 5 with the second, B string 5 with the third, top string 3 with the first.
Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.sevenths.sevenths-in-the-key.ti: One, six, two, five in sevenths
strings.exercise.sevenths.sevenths-in-the-key.pu: C major seven, A minor seven, D minor seven and G seven, each going up from its root on the D string.
strings.exercise.sevenths.sevenths-in-the-key.ho: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. One bar on each chord.
C major seven: 10, 9, 8, 7. A minor seven: 7, 5, 5, 3. D minor seven: 12, 10, 10, 8. G seven: 5, 4, 3, 1. The D string's fret is given first each time.
strings.exercise.sevenths.sevenths-in-the-key.co: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.sevenths.sevenths-in-the-key.de: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.title: A two, five, one line
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.purpose: D minor seven, G seven and two bars of C major seven as one line in eighths, each chord picked up from a note close to where the last one ended.
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.howTo.0: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. The last bar is one long C.
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.howTo.1: Bar 1, D minor seven: D string 12, G string 10, B string 10, top string 8, then top string 10 and 8, B string 10, G string 10.
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.howTo.2: Bar 2, G seven: G string 7, B string 6 and 8, top string 7 and 10, then back: top string 7, B string 8 and 6. Bar 3, C major seven, starts on E, one fret below the F you just played: B string 5 and 8, top string 7 and 8, then top string 7, B string 8 and 5, G string 4. Bar 4: C on the G string, fret 5, held.
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.sevenths.two-five-one.detection: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.step.two-octaves.title: Two octaves
strings.step.two-octaves.goal: Play A minor and C major arpeggios across all six strings, two octaves each.
strings.step.two-octaves.why: One octave fits under the hand; two octaves cross all six strings, and that is the size of arpeggio many solos use. Nothing new is needed to build one: it is root, third, fifth, and then the same three again an octave higher. These two shapes, one minor and one major, both starting from the low E string, are what one family of big sweep shapes is built on.
strings.step.two-octaves.howTo.0: A minor from fret 5 on the low E string: A and C on the low E (frets 5 and 8), E on the A string (7), A on the D string (7), then fret 5 on the G, B and top strings.
strings.step.two-octaves.howTo.1: C major from fret 8 on the low E string: C (8), then E and G on the A string (7 and 10), C on the D string (10), E on the G string (9), G on the B string (8), C on the top string (8).
strings.step.two-octaves.howTo.2: The top half of each is the one-octave shape you already know.
strings.step.two-octaves.howTo.3: Fingers. A minor: first and fourth on the low E string, third on the A string and rolled onto the D string, first finger rolled across fret 5. C major: second on the low E, first and fourth on the A string, fourth rolled onto the D string, second on the G string, first across the B and top strings.
strings.step.two-octaves.payoff: Two arpeggios that cover six strings.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.a-minor-two.title: A minor, two octaves
strings.exercise.two-octaves.a-minor-two.purpose: A, C, E twice over, from the low E string to the top string, and back down to the low A.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.a-minor-two.howTo.0: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Two bars.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.a-minor-two.howTo.1: Up: low E string 5 and 8, A string 7, D string 7, then fret 5 on the G, B and top strings. Down: B string 5, G string 5, D string 7, A string 7, low E string 8, and fret 5 held.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.a-minor-two.coachLi: Right notes and even eighths after the take.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.c-major-two.title: C major, two octaves
strings.exercise.two-octaves.c-major-two.purpose: C, E, G twice over from fret 8 on the low E string, and back down.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.c-major-two.howTo.0: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Two bars.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.c-major-two.howTo.1: Up: low E string 8, A string 7 and 10, D string 10, G string 9, B string 8, top string 8. Down: B string 8, G string 9, D string 10, A string 10 and 7, and the low C held.
strings.exercise.two-octaves.c-major-two.coachLi: Right notes and even eighths after the take.
C and A minor across the neck
Two bars of C major and two of A minor, each a full two-octave arpeggio up and back, with the band.
Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 2 are the C major arpeggio from fret 8 on the low E string. Bars 3 and 4 are A minor from fret 5.
Band on. Right notes and time after the take.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.step.two-octaves-more.title: Two octaves on other chords
strings.step.two-octaves-more.goal: Move the two-octave major shape to G and D and the minor shape to D minor and E minor, and play one, four and five of a key across all six strings.
strings.step.two-octaves-more.why: You learned one major shape on C and one minor shape on A minor. They are not C and A minor shapes: put the first note on another fret of the low E string and you have another chord, exactly as with barre chords. Moving them is what makes them useful, because a song has more than one chord and each one needs its arpeggio where the hand can reach it.
strings.step.two-octaves-more.howTo.0: The major shape starts with the second finger on the root, on the low E string. C is at fret 8, so G is at fret 3 and D is at fret 10.
strings.step.two-octaves-more.howTo.1: The minor shape starts with the first finger on the root. A minor is at fret 5, so D minor is at fret 10 and E minor at fret 12.
strings.step.two-octaves-more.howTo.2: Say the root before you move. The hand goes where the root is, and the rest of the shape comes with it.
strings.step.two-octaves-more.payoff: A two-octave arpeggio for any major or minor chord, from one shape each.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.g-major-two.pu: G, B, D twice over from fret 3 on the low E string, and back down. The C major shape, five frets lower.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.g-major-two.ho: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Two bars.
Up: low E string 3, A string 2 and 5, D string 5, G string 4, B string 3, top string 3. Down: B string 3, G string 4, D string 5, A string 5 and 2, and the low G held.
The frets are wider down here than at fret 8. Let the hand move a little instead of straining to hold every finger over its fret.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.g-major-two.co: Right notes and even eighths after the take.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.d-minor-two.pu: D, F, A twice over from fret 10 on the low E string, and back down to the low D. The A minor shape, five frets higher.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.d-minor-two.ho: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Two bars.
Up: low E string 10 and 13, A string 12, D string 12, then fret 10 on the G, B and top strings. Down: B string 10, G string 10, D string 12, A string 12, low E string 13, and fret 10 held.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.d-minor-two.co: Right notes and even eighths after the take.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.one-four-five-: G, C and D across the neck
One, four and five of the key of G, two bars each and two more of G: the same two-octave shape from fret 3, fret 8, fret 10 and fret 3 again, with the band.
Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Eight bars.
Bars 1 and 2: G from fret 3 on the low E string. Bars 3 and 4: C from fret 8. Bars 5 and 6: D from fret 10. Bars 7 and 8: G from fret 3.
Each arpeggio ends on a held root. Use that note's length to move the hand to the next root.
Eight bars with the band. Right notes and time after the take.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.minor-across.t: A minor, D minor and E minor across the neck
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.minor-across.p: One, four and five of the key of A minor, two bars each and two more of A minor: the minor shape from fret 5, fret 10, fret 12 and fret 5 again.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.minor-across.h: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Eight bars.
Bars 1 and 2: A minor from fret 5 on the low E string. Bars 3 and 4: D minor from fret 10. Bars 5 and 6: E minor from fret 12. Bars 7 and 8: A minor from fret 5.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.minor-across.c: Eight bars with the band. Right notes and time after the take.
strings.exercise.two-octaves-more.minor-across.d: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.step.sevenths-across.title: Sevenths across the neck
strings.step.sevenths-across.goal: Play A minor seven, C major seven and G seven across all six strings, and a two, five, one line that uses the whole width of the neck.
strings.step.sevenths-across.why: The one-octave seventh arpeggios sit on four strings. Add the seventh to the two-octave shapes and you have them across all six, which is how they are used in a solo: a line can start low and arrive high, or the other way, and stay inside the chord the whole time. One of them you half know already. A minor seven is A, C, E and G, and those are four of the five notes of the A minor pentatonic box.
strings.step.sevenths-across.howTo.0: A minor seven from fret 5 on the low E string: the pentatonic box at fret 5 with one note, D, left out. Two notes on the low E, D and B strings, one on the A and G strings, and the A at fret 5 on the top string.
strings.step.sevenths-across.howTo.1: C major seven from fret 8: the C major two-octave shape with a B added just under each C after the first, on the D string at fret 9 and the top string at fret 7.
strings.step.sevenths-across.howTo.2: G seven from fret 3: the G major shape with an F added just under each G after the first, on the D string at fret 3 and the top string at fret 1.
strings.step.sevenths-across.payoff: Three kinds of seventh chord across six strings, and a line that crosses the neck in both directions.
strings.exercise.sevenths-across.a-minor-seven-t: A, C, E, G twice over, from the low E string to the top string, and back down to the A on the D string. It is the pentatonic box you know, with the D left out.
Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Two bars.
Up: low E string 5 and 8, A string 7, D string 5 and 7, G string 5, B string 5 and 8, top string 5. Down: B string 8 and 5, G string 5, and the A on the D string, fret 7, held.
Right notes and even eighths after the take.
strings.exercise.sevenths-across.c-major-seven-t: C, E, G, B twice over from fret 8 on the low E string, up to the high C and back down to the C on the D string.
Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Two bars.

strings.step.a-whole-form.title: Arpeggios through a whole form
strings.step.a-whole-form.goal: Play arpeggios through all twelve bars of a blues in C, move the four-chord line to other keys, and improvise with chord notes only.
strings.step.a-whole-form.why: Four bars can be memorised as finger movements. Twelve cannot: you have to know which chord is coming. This is the Step where the arpeggio stops being a pattern and becomes a way of following a song, and the twelve-bar blues form, which Chords in a Key teaches in its last Level and which is spelled out below, is the best place to practise that.
strings.step.a-whole-form.howTo.0: The form: four bars of C, two of F, two of C, then G, F, C, G.
strings.step.a-whole-form.howTo.1: The jumps between C at fret 10 and F at fret 3 are on purpose here: every bar starts from its root so the form is easy to follow. Joining them up is your-turn work at the end of the Step.

strings.step.a-whole-form.howTo.3: In a new key the roots move and the two shapes do not.
strings.step.a-whole-form.payoff: A twelve-bar chorus made only of chord notes, in time, without getting lost.

strings.step.joined-sevenths.title: Sevenths, joined up
strings.step.joined-sevenths.goal: Play one, six, two, five in seventh chords as a single eighth-note line, move it to other keys, and then make your own.
strings.step.joined-sevenths.why: This is the two ideas of the Path together: four-note chords, and the nearest note at every change. A line like this is what a player means by 'playing the changes'. It is written out so you can feel how it moves, and then it is yours to vary.
strings.step.joined-sevenths.howTo.0: Each bar is eight notes of one chord. The first note of each bar is the last note of the bar before, or the note next to it.
strings.step.joined-sevenths.howTo.1: The line climbs highest in bar 2, to fret 12 on the top string, and comes down through G seven to B, a half step below the C it starts again on. The hand moves back up to fret 10 for the repeat.
strings.step.joined-sevenths.howTo.2: Take it one bar at a time, then two, before you play all four.
strings.step.joined-sevenths.payoff: A four-bar line through four seventh chords that sounds like music and not like a drill.

strings.step.minor-two-five-one.title: Two, five, one in a minor key
strings.step.minor-two-five-one.goal: Play B half-diminished and E seven as arpeggios, join them into a two, five, one line that lands on A minor, and move the line to other minor keys.
strings.step.minor-two-five-one.why: Two, five, one is the way home in a minor key as well, and it sounds darker. In A minor the two chord is built on B, and it comes out half-diminished: B, D, F, A. The five chord is E, turned from minor into a seven chord so that it pulls: E, G sharp, B, D. The G sharp is the one note here from outside the scale, and it sits a fret below A, the note it wants to reach. Playing these arpeggios is the quickest way to hear a minor key's pull.
strings.step.minor-two-five-one.howTo.0: B half-diminished, written Bm7b5: D string 9, G string 7, B string 6, top string 5. It is B, D, F and A.
strings.step.minor-two-five-one.howTo.1: E seven: A string 7, D string 6 and 9, G string 7. It is E, G sharp, B and D.
strings.step.minor-two-five-one.howTo.2: The D on the G string, fret 7, is in both chords. The F of the first chord falls one fret to E, and the A falls one fret to G sharp.
strings.step.minor-two-five-one.payoff: The way home in a minor key, as a line, in four keys.

strings.step.first-sweeps.title: The first sweeps
strings.step.first-sweeps.goal: Play a three-string triad up with one push of the pick and back with one pull, slowly, on A minor and then on four chords.
strings.step.first-sweeps.why: Sweeping is a way of picking an arpeggio: when the notes are on neighbouring strings, the pick does not go down, up, down. It falls through the strings in one slow push, like a strum in slow motion, and comes back in one pull. You know the notes already: they are the triad shapes from Triads. The only new thing is the picking hand, and the only rule is the old one from this Path, that each note lets go as the next one sounds.
strings.step.first-sweeps.howTo.0: Going up, one downward push through the G, B and top strings: the pick comes to rest against each string before it plays it. Coming back, one upward pull.
strings.step.first-sweeps.howTo.1: The top note is played twice, at the end of the push and the start of the pull, and so is the bottom note. Those are the only places the pick changes direction.
strings.step.first-sweeps.howTo.2: Fretting hand: press each note only while it sounds. A sweep where the fingers stay down is a strum. Where the first finger holds two strings, rock it from one to the other. The side of the picking hand rests lightly on the strings you have just left.
strings.step.first-sweeps.howTo.3: Triplets are three even notes to a click.
strings.step.first-sweeps.payoff: A triad in one motion of the pick, clean, at a slow tempo.

strings.step.more-sweeps.title: Two more shapes to sweep
strings.step.more-sweeps.goal: Sweep a triad held by one finger across three strings, sweep the minor shape that has its root lowest, and sweep C, G, A minor and F around fret 5.
strings.step.more-sweeps.why: The first sweeps used shapes where every note has a finger of its own, or nearly. Two more fingerings turn up as soon as you sweep a real progression. One is the triad that is a single finger laid across three strings: there the finger has to roll, pressing one string at a time, or the sweep is just a chord. The other is the minor shape with its root lowest, three fingers on three frets, which is the shape the Sweep Picking Path begins with. The first is in the song in the next Step, and the second is where Sweep Picking will start you, so both get a Step of their own first.
strings.step.more-sweeps.howTo.0: A minor at fret 5 is the first finger across the G, B and top strings. To sweep it, press with the part of the finger under the string being played and let the rest go slack: the part nearest the hand for the G string, then the middle, then the tip for the top string. The finger rocks; it does not lift.
strings.step.more-sweeps.howTo.1: D minor with its root lowest: G string 7 with the third finger, B string 6 with the second, top string 5 with the first. Each finger lifts a little as the next string sounds.
strings.step.more-sweeps.howTo.2: The picking hand does what it did before: one push up through the strings, one pull back, the top and bottom notes played twice.
strings.step.more-sweeps.payoff: The triad fingerings of the song's first four bars, and the shape Sweep Picking starts from, swept slowly and clean.

strings.exercise.more-sweeps.barre-sweep.howTo.2: Rock the finger so only the string you are picking is pressed. If you hear a chord, slow down.

strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.title: Sweeps in a song, and where to go next
strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.goal: Sweep an eight-bar progression in two parts of the neck, in other keys, and play the two-octave A minor arpeggio in triplets.
strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.why: This is the end of the route that began with counting a scale on one string. You know what a chord is, where its notes are, which chords belong together, how to move between them, and how to play them as lines. What is left is speed and bigger shapes, and that is a technique with its own Path: Sweep Picking starts exactly here, with the three-string triad you have just swept, and takes it to five and six strings.
strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.howTo.0: Bars 1 to 4 around fret 5: C is 5, 5, 3. G is 4, 3, 3. A minor is 5, 5, 5. F is 5, 6, 5.
strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.howTo.1: Bars 5 to 8 around fret 8: C is 9, 8, 8. G is 7, 8, 7. A minor is 9, 10, 8. F is 10, 10, 8.
strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.howTo.2: Keep the tempo where every note is separate. Sweep Picking is where it gets faster: it asks for clean hammer-ons and pull-offs and even alternate picking first, and its first Step passes these triads at 100 BPM.
strings.step.sweeps-in-a-song.payoff: An eight-bar song in sweeps, and a clear next Path.
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.song-sweeps.pu: C, G, A minor, F around fret 5 and then around fret 8, each bar a triad swept up and back.
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.song-sweeps.ho: Triplets, 50 BPM up to a pass at 70. One bar on each chord.

The shapes are the song from Triads. There are two shifts: after bar 4, and from bar 8 back to the start. Let the last note before each be short. A minor is one finger rolled across three strings, the hardest shape here to keep clean.
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.song-sweeps.co: Eight bars with the band. Timed and counted; the pitch is for your ear.
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.song-sweeps.de: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.song-sweeps.se: Did each note stop as the next one started, with no two strings ringing together?
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.song-sweeps-ke: The same song in a new key
The eight bars moved along the neck: in D, in E, or in B flat.
Triplets, 50 BPM up to a pass at 70. One bar on each chord.
In D everything is two frets higher than in C: the first shape is G string 7, B string 7, top string 5.
The frets and chord names here are for the first version. On other days the same line comes in another key, higher or lower on the neck.
A key that changes from day to day. Timed and counted; the pitch is for your ear.
Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
Did each note stop as the next one started, with no two strings ringing together?
Triplets, 50 BPM up to a pass at 70. One bar on each chord.
In E, bars 1 to 4, on the G, B and top strings: E is 9, 9, 7. B is 8, 7, 7. C sharp minor is 9, 9, 9. A is 9, 10, 9.
Bars 5 to 8, higher on the neck: E is 13, 12, 12. B is 11, 12, 11. C sharp minor is 13, 14, 12. A is 14, 14, 12.
Triplets, 50 BPM up to a pass at 70. One bar on each chord.
In B flat, bars 1 to 4, on the G, B and top strings: B flat is 3, 3, 1. F is 2, 1, 1. G minor is 3, 3, 3. E flat is 3, 4, 3.
Bars 5 to 8, higher on the neck: B flat is 7, 6, 6. F is 5, 6, 5. G minor is 7, 8, 6. E flat is 8, 8, 6.
strings.exercise.sweeps-in-a-song.two-octaves-in: The two-octave A minor arpeggio, three notes to a beat: up, back down to the low A, and up again to finish on C. From the A string to the top string, going up, the notes fall one to a string, which is where a sweep fits.
Triplets, 50 BPM up to a pass at 70. Two bars.

Up: low E string 5 and 8, A string 7, D string 7, then fret 5 on the G, B and top strings, and top string 8. Then back down the same notes to the low A, and up once more: low E string 8, A string 7, D string 7, and G string 5 held for two beats.
Pick it any way that keeps it even. If you sweep, let each note go as the next sounds.
Timed and counted; the pitch is for your ear.
Did each note stop as the next one started, with no two strings ringing together?
strings.level.beginner.title: Beginner: one chord, one octave
strings.level.beginner.summary: A chord played as a line from its root, an arpeggio for each of four chords, and moving to the nearest note when the chord changes.
strings.level.beginner.startHereIf.0: You can play C, A minor, F and G as triads with the band at 80 BPM.
strings.level.beginner.startHereIf.1: You roll chord shapes and have never played a chord's notes as a line.
strings.level.beginner.startHereIf.2: You can find a chord's root on 1 string.
strings.exercise.warmup-beginner.arpeggios-one-f: The one-octave major arpeggio on the first, fourth and fifth chords of a key and home. A different key each time.
Straight eighths, well under your clean tempo. Find each root on the D string before the bar starts, and let every note go as the next one sounds.
This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.
strings.level.intermediate.title: Intermediate: sevenths, two octaves, a whole form
strings.level.intermediate.summary: Seventh chords as one changed note, a two, five, one line, arpeggios across six strings on six chords, seventh arpeggios across the neck, and twelve bars of chord notes.
strings.level.intermediate.startHereIf.0: You can play one-octave arpeggios through 4 chords at 80 BPM.
strings.level.intermediate.startHereIf.1: You can move from one chord to the next without jumping back to the root.
strings.level.intermediate.startHereIf.2: You have not yet played a seventh chord as an arpeggio.
strings.exercise.warmup-intermediate.sevenths-ro: Four seventh chords, up or down
One, six, two, five in seventh chords, each between its root on the D string and its seventh on the top string, going up one day and coming down another, in a key that changes.
Quarter notes, well under your clean tempo. Say the name of each chord as you start it.
This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.
strings.level.advanced.title: Advanced: playing the changes, and the first sweeps
strings.level.advanced.summary: A line through four seventh chords in more than one key, two, five, one in a minor key, three-string triads swept slowly in four fingerings, an eight-bar song in sweeps, and the hand-off to Sweep Picking.
strings.level.advanced.startHereIf.0: You can play C major seven, A minor seven, D minor seven and G seven as arpeggios at 80 BPM.
strings.level.advanced.startHereIf.1: You can follow a 12-bar form with arpeggios without getting lost.
strings.level.advanced.startHereIf.2: You have never swept, or you sweep fast and can't play the same notes slowly and clean.
strings.exercise.warmup-advanced.slow-sweeps.tit: A slow sweep round three chords
strings.exercise.warmup-advanced.slow-sweeps.pur: One triad shape swept up and back on the first, fourth and fifth chords of a key and home, slowly. A different shape and key each time.
strings.exercise.warmup-advanced.slow-sweeps.how: Triplets, well under your clean tempo. One push up, one pull back, and each note lets go as the next one sounds. The last bar stops on its top note.
strings.exercise.warmup-advanced.slow-sweeps.coa: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.
strings.exercise.warmup-advanced.slow-sweeps.det: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
